title: Why Don't We Fully Understand Our Own Brains?
content_html:
Why Don't We Fully Understand Our Own Brains?

At an intuitive level it is surprising that a creature can reflect, speak, build physics, and yet struggle to understand the organ that makes all of this possible. We carry our brains everywhere; they generate every thought and feeling. The fact that their inner workings remain only partially understood can feel like a paradox, especially if one expects a mind to have transparent access to its own mechanisms.

But that feeling of surprise arises from a particular folk picture of the mind: that we should "just know" what is going on inside, in the same way we know what we are thinking right now. Modern neuroscience and psychology show that this picture is misleading. Introspection gives us access to the contents of thought, not the machinery that produces it.

One reason we do not yet "know how our brains work" in any complete sense is sheer complexity. The human brain contains on the order of 86 billion neurons and a comparable number of glial cells, forming roughly 100 trillion synaptic connections. Each neuron is a complex dynamical system, and their collective interactions generate a combinatorial explosion of possible states and patterns of activity. Mapping the detailed circuitry of even small regions is an enormous technical challenge, spurring new fields like connectomics that attempt to chart the brain's wiring at multiple scales.

Neuroscientists themselves emphasize that such scale is not "a small problem" that can be solved by simple sampling. It requires coordinated advances in measurement, theory, and computation. In that sense, it is perhaps less surprising that, a few decades into modern neuroscience, our understanding is deep in some areas and fragmentary in others.

A second reason is that evolution did not equip us with direct, high-resolution introspective access to our own neural machinery. Classic work by Nisbett and Wilson argued that people have little direct access to the processes that generate their judgments and choices, and instead often construct plausible explanations after the fact. Later "choice blindness" experiments showed that people can fail to notice when their own choices are covertly swapped, yet still provide confident reasons for the choice they think they made.

This does not mean we know nothing about ourselves, but it does mean that the mechanisms of perception, decision, and memory operate largely outside awareness. The brain, left to its own everyday devices, cannot simply "look inside" and read out its code. Scientific understanding requires external instruments, population-level studies, and theoretical frameworks.

A third factor is conceptual. As David Marr and others argued, understanding an information processing system like the brain requires multiple levels of analysis: the level of the computational problem being solved, the algorithms and representations used, and the implementation in physical hardware. It is difficult to infer the right algorithm and representation directly from the neural hardware alone. Behavioural data, computational modelling, and neural recordings all have to be integrated.

Our partial understanding reflects this division of labour. We have made substantial progress on some computational questions (for example, how the visual system infers depth or motion), on some algorithmic proposals (predictive processing, reinforcement learning, attractor networks), and on many aspects of implementation (ion channels, synaptic plasticity, microcircuits). But a complete, unified story that links all three levels for the whole brain is still a work in progress. The surprise comes if one tacitly expects a single, simple "how it works" description.

So rather than "we do not know how our brains work," a more accurate summary might be:

We have a rapidly growing, multi-level understanding of many brain subsystems and principles, but no finite system can be fully transparent to itself, and the complexity of the human brain makes a complete, unified explanation an ongoing scientific project rather than a finished product.

From this angle, it becomes less surprising that the brain that uses simplified self-models in everyday life also requires sophisticated external tools and collective inquiry to understand itself scientifically.
